questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] splitting one column into two new tables on a live product (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/07). The issue tracker keeps labels as a text array on the Issue row: 3.4M issues carrying about 8.5M label assignments, around 650 writes/s at peak, and the business tolerates only about 300 ms of blocked writes. The target is a Label table (one row per project and name) plus an IssueLabel join table, after which the array column is dropped for good. Label search filters on labels, deploys are rolling with migrations run in a release phase, and a mobile client that ships monthly still sends the whole label array on every edit. Write your plan before you look: how the new tables and their constraints arrive without stalling writes, how one array row becomes many rows and how you prove the two shapes agree, which writers can bypass the new tables and how you catch their writes, when search moves over, and which step can never be undone and what you keep before taking it. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] The copy is a fan-out, not a column copy: each distinct label name per project becomes one Label row and each issue-label pair one IssueLabel row, with uniqueness on the natural keys (project + name, issue + label) so that re-running a batch, or overlapping with live writes, converges instead of duplicating.

[w3] Agreement is proven issue by issue, not by totals: for every issue the set of names rebuilt from the join must equal the array, with case variants, repeated entries and NULL versus an empty array each given an explicit rule, and the comparison is run after the copy and again right before reads move.

[w3] The drop is named as the one irreversible step: once the array stops being maintained it goes stale, and dropping it deletes the only copy of the old shape, so an archive of the column is taken first and anything after that point is fixed forward, not rolled back.

[w2] DDL that touches the busy Issue table runs under a short lock_timeout, because a statement queued behind a long transaction makes every later write queue behind it; constraints added after the new tables are full go on NOT VALID and are validated in a separate step.

[w2] Old binaries and the monthly mobile client keep writing labels only into the array, so a sweep (or a trigger) re-copies every issue whose array changed after the backfill, until the last writer of the old shape is gone.
keyPoints.quote: after the migration has already run

keyPoints.text: [w2] Label search moves to the join tables as its own switchable step, with the supporting index on the join table in place first, while the array is still maintained so search can be pointed back at it.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the split ships like this: the copy is one INSERT ... SELECT inside the release-phase migration; old machines keep saving label edits for twenty minutes after it ran; the agreement check compared total row counts and was tested on a freshly seeded database; dropping the array goes out in the same release that moves reads to the new tables; the join table's foreign key is added fully validated after the load; and the next day someone asks for a rollback. What breaks, who notices first, and what in your plan already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A single fan-out statement in the migration holds one huge transaction and its locks for the whole copy, stalls the deploy behind it, and cannot resume: a failure halfway throws all of it away and starts over.

[w3] Label edits saved by old machines after the copy exist only in the array; once reads move they vanish from issue views and search with no error, which is the silent-loss shape of a split rather than a crash.
keyPoints.quote: silent data loss when the old code writes a column the new code no longer reads

keyPoints.text: [w3] A total-count check on clean seed data passes while real issues disagree: production arrays hold case variants, repeats and NULL-versus-empty that the seed never had, so counts can match while individual issues lost or gained labels.
keyPoints.quote: Any test that starts from an empty database passes too.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Shipping the drop with the read switch leaves no release in which both shapes exist: the previous binary fails the moment it is rolled back to, and labels written since live only in the new tables, so next day's rollback becomes a data rebuild, not a redeploy.
keyPoints.quote: must be compatible with the currently running version

keyPoints.text: [w2] A foreign key added fully validated to a loaded table scans every row while holding a lock that blocks writes on both tables, so the release stalls writes far past the 300 ms budget.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your split against the alternatives: keeping the array maintained through the window vs cutting over early, application dual-writes vs a database trigger that keeps both shapes in step, a batched resumable copy vs one statement, archiving the column before the drop vs dropping it straight away, and splitting inside one database vs moving labels into a separate service. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Keeping the array current until the new tables are trusted makes undo a plain redeploy, at the price of doubled label writes, more storage and a longer migration window; cutting over early is cheaper only if you accept that undo means rebuilding data.
keyPoints.quote: wait one full release so rollback stays safe

keyPoints.text: [w3] A trigger catches writes from every path, including binaries that know nothing of the new tables, but hides logic in the database, adds work to every write on a hot table and must itself be removed safely; application dual-writes are visible and testable but miss the old binaries.
[w2] A batched copy with a checkpoint is slower to finish and needs code to track progress, but keeps each transaction and its locks small and can be stopped, throttled and resumed under peak load.
[w2] Archiving the column before the drop costs storage and an extra step, and buys the only way to answer 'what were this issue's labels before the split' once the column is gone.

[w2] Inside one database the old and new shapes can be written in one transaction; moving labels to another service loses that, so the copy and the dual-write become an event stream with lag, and agreement checks have to tolerate in-flight differences.
